summary: A document cannot be read as it stood, or as it will stand, on a date: eta has no valid_from, valid_to
detail: Carried forward from Genoa (2013, ~/Workshop/archive/post-peleton/Genoa/src/genoa/core/valid_from_valid_to.py), where hedge-fund use needed 'what did we believe on the 3rd'. Genoa's shape: an update closes the current row (valid_to = now) and inserts a new one under the same `ref`; `valid_on(date)` filters any query; many-to-many relations carry their own valid range; `find_or_create` on a date respects a version already dated in the future. Two kinds of time are involved, and eta has only one. Transaction time (when a write was recorded) is the ledger's -- delta's `delta_ledger`: ops, inverse and `at` per entry, so a document registered with the ledger can already be walked back to any moment, but only while the recorded paths still mean what they meant before the schema changed. Valid time (when something is true in the world: a price effective from Monday, a deal term that changes next quarter) is what Genoa's valid_from/valid_to gave and the ledger cannot, because it is written now about later. Design questions: (a) derive as-at reads from the ledger, with no schema change, or (b) put valid_from/valid_to on the tables and give a document's read() an `at`, or both, one for each kind of time; (c) name it as delta did, with the date in the document's name (`venue-at:42:2026-06-16`), so an as-at document is read-only and seen like any other; (d) how undo treats a future-dated write. Start with a story, per CLAUDE.md, not a feature: stories.md's Open 'Time' (the wedding's deadline, a story with a `when`) is where it meets the harness.
note: 2026-09-24: added after comparing eta with Genoa/Landfall (~/Workshop/archive/post-peleton/overview.md). Open, for Peter. 2026-09-25 review: lowered to low: no story needs it yet; delta already reads a temporal table as it stood (openAt), and eta turns temporal off -- what is missing is a value that takes effect later.

summary: No page is drawn from a document's shape: every view is placed by hand, and nothing lets a named component override a type's drawing
detail: The second thing carried forward from Genoa/Landfall (~/Workshop/archive/post-peleton/overview.md), and the thread the line has kept picking up. Landfall (2013): Genoa's describe_model() published every model's properties and types; `{label, model}` in ui.js gave a working list/view/edit panel; each value's template was looked up by `<mode>-<type>` (viewcell, editcell, inlinecell, viewfield, editfield), last registered wins, so one override changed every Image column; the settings, then a custom `js` panel, went further. It is what let Betts and Gilbert build fund screens without the architect, and most of Gilbert's 102 commits went into those generic screens. Since then: zeta DEC-10 (13 Sep 2026) derived a screen from a TypeScript `Table` that a test checks against the live schema (`zeta/describe.ts` is Genoa's describe.py again), with few rules in `zeta/derive.ts` and anything beyond them a hand-written node; apples' panel: every row has one, derived from the declaration, the same panel from every reading; hjeli's derive-ux in an earlier app. eta has the pieces but no derivation: bento's boxPage/collectionPage, `choice`, `row`, `cell`; applets registered by name (`registerApplet`, last wins, the same mechanism as data-micro) but placed by hand in each view (the wedding's picture-field is Landfall's editfield-image again). The tension is with eta's own rules: 'Build nothing no story needs', 'Not generated code', and the 17 Sep review's YAGNI D. So derive at render time, never generate files; derive from the document (what read() returns, or a declaration the database vouches for, as zeta did), never from the entity; let a type name an applet, so an override is a registration, not an edit to every view. Questions: (a) what a document declares about itself (types, labels, which paths are writable, which the permit already says); (b) whether the permit table and the page come from the same declaration; (c) where the override ladder stops, and write it down: Landfall's most powerful hooks (type templates, swapping controls, page blocks) were never documented; (d) the evidence: which screens did Landfall's users actually live in, custom or generic? Start with a story no example tells yet: reference data nobody would write a story for, e.g. 'The couple add a venue, and it is in the list' with no view written for venues.
note: 2026-09-24: added after comparing eta with Genoa/Landfall. Open, for Peter.

summary: Paging and streaming: no story yet reads past the first page or receives a result over time
detail: Landfall (2013) had it from the start: genoa_list(model, criteria, offset, limit, summary, order_by) answered {items, count, summary}; table_limit 24 on a desktop, 10 on a phone, -1 for all; a pagination template; per-collection limits; totals (sum, avg) worked out over the whole filtered set, not the page. eta today: chat holds a room whole in memory, as one delta document, and shows its last 50 messages (documents/room.ts), so more is held than before and nothing reaches older ones; bento's find dims and counts, never hides, so a filter doesn't reduce what is sent; every write redraws each reader's whole page on the server and diffs it against the page last sent, which server.ts keeps per connection, so cost grows with page size times readers. concept found whole-document transport breaks at ~5k records, and concept/scale.md has real sizes (85k allocations, 40k areas). Two things, related: PAGING, a window onto a collection, and STREAMING, rows arriving over time (a feed, a long result from a Bun `$` callout or an outside queue written back as facts, a slow first page). Much of the machinery exists: doc names are data, and compartment.ts already expects 'one whose name is criteria (this month's appointments, last month's)'; the address (`path?what=which`) could carry the window, so the back button pages; parts.ts already sends rows added to or removed from a list as `after`/`before`/`remove`, which is the wire shape of streaming. Questions: (a) the window in the document's name (`room:general?before=812`) or in the tray's address; (b) who is told: a write lands on `room:general`, and reading() records the name the page read, so a window's readers are told only if the window reads its base document too, or the kernel learns that one name belongs to a family of names; (c) keyset (before=id) or offset: an offset moves under a concurrent insert (room.ts line 31 uses LIMIT 1 OFFSET), a keyset does not; (d) totals and counts over the whole set are a read of their own, as the wedding's counts already are; (e) the harness: a cast whose pages are windows, and `seen`/`unseen` for someone who has scrolled away. Stories to start from: 'Ada scrolls back past the first fifty messages and reads what Bob said yesterday'; 'Bob speaks while Ada is reading old messages, and her place does not move'.
note: 2026-09-24: added after comparing eta with Genoa/Landfall. Distributed work itself is out of scope (Bun `$` or a queue, not eta or delta); only how its result arrives belongs here. Open, for Peter.

summary: Stale writes: two people changing one value, and the last write silently wins
detail: Genoa (2013) had optimistic locking: a `Versioned` model carried `_version_`, a save sent the version it was based on, and `from_pairs` raised 'Version mismatch' on a stale one (Genoa/src/genoa/access/versioned.py). An eta write carries no base version, and PatchOp is add, replace and remove only, so two people replacing one path both land, in arrival order, and the first never learns it was overwritten. `data-write-on="input"` (debounced, K3) makes it likelier: a field is written while someone else reads it. RFC 6902 already has the guard: a `test` op, which fails the whole patch unless the value at the path is what the writer saw; eta's three verbs stay three, and `test` is a condition, not a change. Alternatives: the version the page was drawn at, sent with the write and checked against the document's version (coarser: any write to the document refuses, not just one to the same path). Questions: (a) `test` per path or version per document; (b) what the refused writer sees (see n5); (c) whether undo and redo, which apply a recorded inverse, carry a test of their own, since walking back over someone else's later write is the same problem; (d) the harness needs two members writing one path. Story: 'Ann and Bob both change the notional; Bob's is refused, and he sees Ann's.'
note: 2026-09-24: from the Genoa/Landfall comparison. Open, for Peter.

summary: Whose history: the ledger records per document, so a row written through two documents has its history split
detail: Genoa (2013) audited per row: Audit held the entity's type and primary key, before-values, what changed and who, for every create, update, delete and many-to-many add or remove, whichever screen made the change, and get_audit_trail(obj) answered 'what happened to this deal'. eta's ledger is keyed by document (`<docType>:<docId>`), with ops as JSON Pointer paths into that document. When one row can be written through two documents, its history is split: in the wedding, a claim (`wedding_claims`) is made through a household and removed through the couple's board when its gift is deleted, and guests and ask replies are written through both, so one row's history is under `board:…` and `household:…`, at different paths. An auditor, or 'why is the casserole the Okafors'?', asks about the thing, not the screen. Options: (a) a rule: every row has exactly one owning document, and other documents only read it (documents-history.md's open question 5, 'every field has exactly one writing actor', said again for rows), which the harness or a test could check; (b) a ledger index by entity: patch() reports the rows it touched alongside the ops, so history can be asked by row; (c) accept it and let history be asked across documents by a join the example writes. It also affects n1: reading a row as it stood on a date needs to know where its history is. Story: 'The couple ask who claimed the casserole and when, and see the Okafors' claim and Ben's withdrawn one.'
note: 2026-09-24: from the Genoa/Landfall comparison. Related to n1. Open, for Peter. 2026-09-25 review: lowered to low: no story asks for it yet.

detail: At 0.46.0 the README's 'Why eta' said 'a chat message is 425 bytes to each other member, a price tick 104' while its Cost section said 804 B and 111 B; on delta a run gives 1,111 B and 186 B, which the README's 'What a write costs' now says, copied by hand (24 Sep). The README already says of story counts 'a number in a README goes stale and a run does not'. Do the same for bytes: the measure scripts write the tables (or a check fails when the README's numbers differ from a run), and prose quotes no number the tables don't.

summary: Identity is not pluggable: every connection is an anonymous visit, and an example cannot refuse an upgrade at /ws or attach a verified identity (the database today, OAuth2 or LDAP tomorrow)
detail: Authorization is already pluggable (permit, own, resolveDoc and reading(), Example.active); authentication is not. server.ts's `/ws` takes the `session_id` cookie or makes a random UUID and upgrades; ConnectionData is `{ sessionId }`; an example cannot refuse an upgrade or attach a verified identity, and cannot replace /ws ('a kernel route of the same path wins'). Every connection is an anonymous visit, and logging in is a write to the session document that the example's compartment judges: the wedding checks an invitation code (`replace /code`, kindOf) against its tables; chat's `/name` is no authentication at all. That is the database as the identity provider, done per example. It is fine for a shared code and wrong for a password: a password sent as a patch sits in the client's `window.eta.inspect().lastSent` and op log and may be echoed to the session's tabs. Genoa (2013) had the same split: AccessControl._login_ against the Person table, then Robert Betts's LDAPMixin overriding _login_ with an LDAP bind (Genoa/src/genoa/access/ldap_mixin.py): one method, swapped. The shape for eta: a provider is (1) HTTP routes on Example.routes (db or LDAP: POST /login with credentials; OAuth2: GET /login redirecting with state and PKCE, GET /callback exchanging the code with fetch and verifying the id_token), and (2) what they all end with: a verified identity and roles, a FRESH session_id cookie (never the pre-login one: session fixation), and the session document written server-side through the example's own document patch() and notify(), with its identity and role paths refused over the wire by permit(). The kernel's one new seam: an optional `Example.identify(req)` called at /ws before the upgrade, returning the session id to use or a Response to refuse, so an example can require a login, accept a reverse proxy's header (SSO), or take a bearer token from the CLI (which keeps `.eta-session` today and would need to log in too). Per provider: db passwords with Bun.password (argon2/bcrypt, built in; Genoa used salted SHA-1); OAuth2 needs no dependency beyond fetch and crypto.subtle for JWKS (or `jose`, to ask about); LDAP needs a client (`ldapts`, to ask about, and a spike under Bun). Questions: (a) identity only in the session document (eta's way), or also on ConnectionData; (b) logout: clear the cookie, delete the visit, close the sockets; (c) one provider per example, or several (codes for guests, OAuth2 for the couple); (d) the harness: casts log in through the provider, or seed sessions with roles and test the provider on its own (a test directory in Docker, a fake OAuth2 issuer). Stories: 'A visitor without a login sees only the login page and cannot write'; 'Ann logs in and sees her desk'; 'Ann cannot give herself the admin role'.

summary: eta keeps its own JSON Pointer parse (it can go now) and applyPatch (it waits on delta #4) beside delta core's
detail: The pointer half can go now: delta 0.7.0's splitPath is strict RFC 6901 (it throws on a slashless path or a stray ~, and '/' is no longer the root), at least as strict as eta's parsePointer, and joinPath / escapeSegment build paths from ids. The swap is mechanical, across src/json-pointer.ts and about 12 example files. The applyPatch half waits on delta #4: delta core's applyOps sets a missing member on replace, ignores a missing remove and overwrites on add at an index, while eta's applyPatch throws on the first two and inserts on the third, and the harness relies on that throw (an applet sent ops that do not describe its props). Swap PatchOp for DeltaOp with it. The shared test vectors that would pin the two together are delta #15 (was eta #22).
note: 2026-09-24: waits on delta core. 2026-09-25 review: the pointer half is unblocked by delta 0.7.0; eta #22 (a wire law and shared vectors) is merged here and into delta #15.

summary: A write carries no id, so no echo can say 'yours'
detail: A form now clears as it sends and a refusal (the page whole before the echo) hands back what was sent (b198341), so no echo resets a field. Left: a whole render that comes for another reason while a write is in flight (someone else's write turns this page into another) is taken for a refusal and puts the sent text back; and eta.inspect().lastSent.echoed matches by document name, so anyone's echo marks it. Fix: `{id?, doc, ops}` on the wire, the id echoed to its writer and a refusal answered `{type: 'refused', id, reason?}` (pairs with n5).

summary: One document named by a live session's id stops the telling of its change to everyone

summary: No shared blueshed plugin or router skill tells an agent which of eta, delta and railroad to use, and delta-doc's own description captures every 'live multi-user app' request before railroad or eta are considered
detail: architect.md §5: delta-doc's SKILL.md claims every 'live multi-user app' request (its description names greenfield apps choosing between Firebase, Supabase and the rest, and the body says 'the answer is delta-doc') and never mentions eta or railroad by name as an alternative; eta-app only fires inside the eta repo, so a greenfield 'build me a live app' request never reaches it even though eta's own README pitches exactly that. Proposed shape (architect §6.2, proposal-final §5): one `blueshed` plugin in a marketplace repo holding a router skill under about 800 words (the decision guide: different people see different slices of the same data, undo matters, forms and lists, one box -> eta; interaction-heavy UI, several processes, Postgres/RLS, other clients consuming the doc JSON -> delta + railroad; one very interactive widget inside eta -> an applet, optionally a railroad island; reactive UI with no sync -> railroad alone), plus WIRE.md, one sandbox hook, one release command and MCP wiring; package skills stay inside the npm packages, synced at session start, restricted to @blueshed/* plus an allowlist (delta's install-skills does this since 02b1926), and delta-doc's own description narrows to projects that have already chosen delta. Namespacing under `blueshed:` ends skill/command shadowing in multi-repo sessions (architect F2, now largely moot since delta re-syncs its vendored railroad skills at each railroad release) and retires each repo's own /publish once `release` lands. Same item in railroad's, delta's and eta's todo.jsonl. The plugin is also the home for shared test tooling (was railroad #14): the two-tab / waitFor browser-test helper is hand-copied in bun-route's reference.md, railroad's tests/webview.test.ts and a dogfooder's tests; eta's src/webview.ts (`at`, `waitFor`) is the tidied version. Ship it as a file in the skill, never a railroad export (it uses Bun types).

summary: A story never uses the page: the harness sends `does` straight down the socket, so a story with no control on any page passes
detail: Every story's write goes from the harness to the server as a message; nothing looks for the control on the author's page, so a story a person cannot do passes (the review of 17 Sep found three wedding stories with no control on any page). The check: before sending, find on the author's open page the element whose data-write matches the story's doc, op and path (and value, where the control carries one), and fail 'X has no control for this on their page' if there is none; better still, drive it (click, fill, submit) as the browser tests do. Then the echo is observed landing: the row changed, by that session.
note: 2026-09-25: from the survey of every completeness check from dzql to eta.

summary: A `does` can be refused and pass, and a `cannot` can pass a write that was allowed but changed nothing
detail: A story with an empty `seen` asks nobody to notice, so its write can be refused and nothing fails; a `cannot` checks that no page changed and the ledger did not move, which a permitted write that changes nothing also satisfies (Ada re-entering the room she is in). A `does` should fail when nothing landed (no ledger entry, no patch to anyone, or the writer handed the page back); a `cannot` should fail unless the write was refused (the page handed back to the writer as a refusal).
note: 2026-09-25: from the survey of every completeness check from dzql to eta. 2026-09-25 review: partly done: a `cannot` with `told` must now show its reason (83dc6dc), but 1 of 20 `cannot` stories uses it, a `cannot` without `told` still passes on a write that was allowed and changed nothing, and a `does` that lands nothing still passes. Telling a refusal from a no-op needs #14's `{type: 'refused'}` on the wire.

summary: Only the named are asked: a cast member in neither `seen` nor `unseen` is never checked
detail: The harness asks `seen` to notice and `unseen` not to, and leaves everyone else alone ('a home page with counts on it changes for many reasons'). So 'Alpha ticks, and Bo, not watching it, notices nothing' never checks Bo: with Bo added to `unseen` it fails ('bo noticed, and should not have'), and so does `fresh`. Either every member is classed seen or unseen, or a member left out is at least told of no document by the write.
note: 2026-09-25: from the survey of every completeness check from dzql to eta. 2026-09-25 review: raised to medium: run with `unseen: ["bo"]`, the ticker's 'Alpha ticks, and Bo, not watching it, notices nothing' fails -- Bo is told of ticker:market -- so a story with a false title passes.

summary: Nothing checks that a control is offered if and only if its write is allowed
detail: Both directions are unchecked: a write the server accepts that no story tells and no page offers (a hidden verb), and a control a page draws whose write is refused (a button that always fails). stories.md defers the first ('a permitted write no story tells is flagged') until a model exists. A start: collect every data-write each member's pages offer during the stories, and fail on one the server refused when sent, and on a permitted path with no story.
note: 2026-09-25: from the survey of every completeness check from dzql to eta.

summary: The fresh render compared against each page reads the server's own copy of the documents, not the database
detail: Canon 2 compares each member's page with a fresh render, but that render reads the same held copy the server draws from ('must see the same copy'), so a copy that drifted from the tables is compared with itself. A fresh read of each document from delta (a new open) for the comparison would make it the law: what each person holds equals what the tables say.
note: 2026-09-25: from the survey of every completeness check from dzql to eta.

summary: A gesture that moves several documents is not one transaction: what `changed()` and `wrote()` write commits after the write
detail: A write and its ledger entry commit together, but the writes that follow from it (who is here, the wedding's everyone, closing an answered modal) are separate transactions, so a failure between them leaves one done and the other not, and another process can see the first alone.
note: 2026-09-25: from the survey of every completeness check from dzql to eta.

summary: There is no way for an applet to ask the server a question: no lookup
detail: The wire has writes and inspect. A search over a large list, a lookup another service answers, or anything the page did not draw cannot be asked: the ticker's city picker ships all ~400 time zones as HTML options because it cannot ask. zeta routed lookups through the server (DEC-2), answered for the socket's own person only (DEC-11). A read-only, permitted, named lookup an applet may call, its answer to that socket alone.
note: 2026-09-25: from the survey of every completeness check from dzql to eta. 2026-09-25 review: lowered to low: no story needs it yet.

summary: /ws accepts a socket opened from any site: no Origin allowlist
detail: A WebSocket is not bound by the same-origin policy. The SameSite=Lax session cookie keeps most cross-site sockets from carrying the session, but the standard defence is an allowlist of origins checked before the upgrade (epsilon's EPSILON_ORIGINS). Related to #8 (an example cannot refuse an upgrade at /ws).
note: 2026-09-25: from the survey of every completeness check from dzql to eta. 2026-09-25 review: lowered to low: sessions are anonymous and the cookie is SameSite=Lax, so a cross-site socket is a new visitor; medium again once #8 (identity) lands.

summary: The ticker's browser test fails now and then under the full suite
detail: 'the board applet takes a tick from the patch itself -- no render -- and the clock runs on its own' failed once in six full runs of bun test on macOS (25 Sep) and passes alone every time: a timing race with the feed or the view under load.
note: 2026-09-25: from the survey of every completeness check from dzql to eta.

summary: Live documents are computed in one process's memory
detail: Who is here, the list of rooms and the wedding's everyone are kept by `changed()` in the process that saw the write, in delta's memory documents. A second process would keep its own and disagree. On Postgres they need either delta telling writes across documents and processes, or views that recompose on what they read.
note: 2026-09-25: from the survey of every completeness check from dzql to eta.

summary: The find field shows no focus
detail: `.filter input:focus-visible { outline: none }` (bento.css) and `outline: none` on the mock-up's filter input, with no `.filter:focus-within` ring in its place. A keyboard user cannot see they are in the field (WCAG 2.4.7). Draw the ring on `.filter:focus-within`.
note: 2026-09-25: from the CSS review of paintbrush, simple, zeta, duckdown and eta.

summary: Buttons have no focus rule of their own
detail: `.tool`, the stack buttons and `.sheet-close` fall back to the browser's default ring, which can vanish on a pressed (accent) background; the trail's links show focus only as an underline. One `:focus-visible` rule for every control, as zeta (`:is(input, button, …):focus-visible`) and duckdown (`:focus-visible { outline: 2px solid var(--accent); outline-offset: 2px }`) have.
note: 2026-09-25: from the CSS review of paintbrush, simple, zeta, duckdown and eta.

summary: In forced colours a chosen thing or row shows nothing
detail: `.thing[aria-pressed]` is marked only by an inset box-shadow, `.row[aria-pressed]` by a shadow and a background; Windows High Contrast removes both, so the selection disappears. No stylesheet in the lineage has `@media (forced-colors: active)`. Add one that outlines what is pressed or chosen in `Highlight`.
note: 2026-09-25: from the CSS review of paintbrush, simple, zeta, duckdown and eta.

summary: Opening a compartment animates under reduced motion
detail: The sheet and the modal drop their animation under `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`; `::view-transition-group(*)` (260ms) and the rails' `transition: right, padding-right` do not.
note: 2026-09-25: from the CSS review of paintbrush, simple, zeta, duckdown and eta.

summary: Field and control borders are below 3:1
detail: Fields and stacks are edged in `--edge`, e.g. chat's rgba(11,61,11,0.28) on white, about 1.7:1. WCAG 1.4.11 asks 3:1 for the boundary of a control. Darken `--edge` in each example, or give fields a second cue.
note: 2026-09-25: from the CSS review of paintbrush, simple, zeta, duckdown and eta.

summary: Reconnecting is not announced, nor are changes from others
detail: "Reconnecting…" is `#app[data-offline]::before` content, which screen readers do not reliably read. It belongs in the HTML as a `role="status"` region. The wider question: a change from someone else morphs into the page silently; decide what, if anything, a live region says.
note: 2026-09-25: from the CSS review of paintbrush, simple, zeta, duckdown and eta.

summary: Text is sized in px
detail: Every font size is px (444 px values to 26 rem/em across eta's stylesheets), so the reader's default font size is ignored (zoom still works), and 13 rules set 11–12px text. A rem type scale as tokens, as simple had (`--font-size-sm` …); keep the 16px floor on fields.
note: 2026-09-25: from the CSS review of paintbrush, simple, zeta, duckdown and eta.

summary: .sr-only uses the deprecated clip
detail: `clip: rect(0,0,0,0)` → `clip-path: inset(50%)`, with `margin: -1px; border: 0; padding: 0`.
note: 2026-09-25: from the CSS review of paintbrush, simple, zeta, duckdown and eta.

summary: The find bar's buttons are 26px, below the kernel's own --touch
detail: `.filter .tool` and `.cell-back` are 26px; they pass WCAG 2.5.8 (24px) but not eta's `--touch` (40px) or the 44px of 2.5.5. Enlarge the hit area (padding or a pseudo-element) without changing the drawing.
note: 2026-09-25: from the CSS review of paintbrush, simple, zeta, duckdown and eta.

summary: No cascade layers: examples fight the kernel by specificity
detail: bento.css is imported first and examples override it by out-specifying or `!important` (the wedding's reduced-motion rules, the ticker's). `@layer kernel, example;` lets an example win by order, and most `!important`s go.
note: 2026-09-25: from the CSS review of paintbrush, simple, zeta, duckdown and eta.

summary: Dark mode duplicates every token, and --ink-rgb is a hack
detail: Each example writes its tokens twice (a `prefers-color-scheme: dark` block). Chat's dark sets `--ink-rgb: 0,0,0` so shadows stay black, bending a token named for ink. `light-dark()` writes each once; `color-mix()` / relative colour derives the translucent, hover and pressed shades from `--ink` and `--accent`, so `--ink-rgb` and `--card-hover` go, and shadows get their own colour token.
note: 2026-09-25: from the CSS review of paintbrush, simple, zeta, duckdown and eta.

summary: Physical sides, not logical properties
detail: `right`, `left`, `padding-left`, `border-right` throughout (98 physical sides, 0 logical). `inset-inline-end`, `padding-inline-start` … make right-to-left a `dir` attribute on the server's HTML.
note: 2026-09-25: from the CSS review of paintbrush, simple, zeta, duckdown and eta.

summary: Compartments respond to the window, not their cell
detail: The 820px breakpoint is repeated 8 times, and what is inside a compartment adapts to the viewport though its cell may be a third of it. `container-type: inline-size` on `.cell` and `@container` for its contents; the tray itself may stay a media query.
note: 2026-09-25: from the CSS review of paintbrush, simple, zeta, duckdown and eta.

summary: Small modern wins not taken
detail: `text-wrap: balance` on headings and `pretty` on prose; `accent-color: var(--accent)` for checkboxes and radios; `scrollbar-gutter: stable` so the page does not jump when a drawer locks scrolling; `:user-invalid` to show a required field refused before the save (proof rule P4) natively.
note: 2026-09-25: from the CSS review of paintbrush, simple, zeta, duckdown and eta.

summary: Nothing checks the examples' colours for contrast
detail: Text contrast passes today (4.9–9.6:1, checked by hand for muted and accent on card, and card on accent) but nothing keeps it so. A test over each example's tokens, light and dark: text pairs at 4.5:1, control edges at 3:1.
